explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The command is plain: “Prepare the nations against her.” The banner and the ram's horn are all pointed at one target. Next the passage starts naming who gets called up.

I see why you'd pick it, but the words are “against her,” not “for her.” Nobody is being called to stand on Babylon's walls. The banner goes up so the nations will be prepared against her. That makes this a summons with a different target than your answer.

Nobody here is picking up a trowel, friend. The nations are summoned against her, and the LORD's intention is “to make the land of Babylon a desolation, without inhabitant.” That's a few verses down, and it points the opposite direction from rebuilding. This horn is calling for battle.

That's the one, baker. The passage says, “the kings of the Medes, their governors and all their officials, and all the lands they rule.” The Medes are a kingdom called up alongside the others. Notice the list reaches past the kings to their officials and the lands they rule.

Egypt is a real nation, friend, but this passage never calls its kings. The text names “the kings of the Medes” here. Their governors, officials and lands are called up with them (Jeremiah 51:28). Egypt just isn't on this guest list.

Assyria is a good guess, since it's a name you hear in the Bible. But it isn't named in these verses. The passage says “the kings of the Medes” get prepared, along with their governors, officials and all the lands they rule. Keep your eyes on that name.

True, baker. The passage says, “The earth quakes and writhes because the LORD’s intentions against Babylon stand…” The reason is right there in the verse. The LORD's intentions stand, and the earth shakes.

This one is true, friend, so the statement matches the text. The verse says, “The earth quakes and writhes because the LORD’s intentions against Babylon stand…” The earth shaking and the LORD's intentions standing are tied together in that one sentence. Hold onto that "because."
Right, baker. The LORD's intentions are “to make the land of Babylon a desolation, without inhabitant.” That means an empty, ruined land with no one living in it. The verse says it plainly.

explanations.answer: A province ruled by the Medes
explanations.explanation: The Medes do show up in this passage, so I get the pull. But nothing here says the land becomes a province under anybody. The LORD says He will make it “a desolation, without inhabitant.” A land with no inhabitants has nobody to rule.

explanations.answer: A city of refuge for nations
explanations.explanation: A city of refuge would be a nice ending, friend, but that's not what the verse says. The LORD's intentions are to make Babylon's land “a desolation, without inhabitant.” Nations are streaming at Babylon with weapons, not looking for shelter. This one is not a welcome mat.
That's it, baker. The verse says, “the bars of her gates are broken.” The warriors are sitting in their strongholds while the city's gates stand broken. The picture is a city that can't be locked.
Towers sound right for a fortress, friend. But this verse says nothing about towers. It says, “the bars of her gates are broken.” Bars are what hold gates shut, and these are broken.

The verse doesn't mention temples here. It says the bars of her gates are broken. Bars belong on gates, because they're what keeps a gate shut. Here those bars are broken, so the gates won't hold anyone out.

explanations.answer: His city has been captured from end to end
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The messengers come “to announce to the king of Babylon that his city has been captured from end to end.” The news covers the whole city, not just one corner. And one courier after another keeps coming with it.

explanations.answer: His army has won the battle at the walls
explanations.explanation: That's the news the king would love to get, friend. But the verse says the opposite. The messengers announce “that his city has been captured from end to end.” Nothing in this passage says his army wins.

explanations.answer: His enemies have turned around and gone home
explanations.explanation: Nice dream, baker, but nobody's packing up. The nations were summoned against Babylon, and the messengers carry news that the king's city “has been captured from end to end.” Captured means the opposite of left alone. Those couriers are not carrying good news.

This one is false, friend. The verse says, “The fords have been seized, the marshes set on fire, and the soldiers are terrified.” Terrified is the opposite of calm. Seized fords and burning marshes will do that to people.
Correct, baker. The text says the soldiers are terrified. The verse reads, “The fords have been seized, the marshes set on fire, and the soldiers are terrified.” Nobody is staying calm in that scene.

Yes, baker. The LORD says, “In just a little while her harvest time will come.” A threshing floor is where harvested grain gets worked, so the word fits the picture. And the time he gives is “just a little while.”

Planting is a good farm word, friend, but it's not the one here. The LORD says, “In just a little while her harvest time will come.” Planting is for the start of the season. This verse is talking about the end, when the crop comes in.

A rest sounds peaceful, baker, but this verse isn't that kind of picture. The LORD says, “In just a little while her harvest time will come.” The threshing floor is being trampled. Nobody is putting their feet up.

explanations.answer: He has devoured and crushed her
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. The speaker says, “Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has devoured me; he has crushed me.” The one speaking is called the dweller of Zion and Jerusalem a verse later. I think this is a heavy line, and it's okay to let it be heavy.

explanations.answer: He has protected and fed her
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what she says, friend. In the passage she says, “he has devoured me; he has crushed me.” She goes on to say he set her aside like an empty vessel. This is a complaint, and a painful one.

explanations.answer: He has freed and honored her
explanations.explanation: No freedom or honor in her words, baker. The speaker says Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, “has devoured me; he has crushed me.” Then she says he set her aside “like an empty vessel.” She is describing being hurt, not honored.

That's right, baker. She says, “May the violence done to me and to my flesh be upon Babylon,” and then adds, “May my blood be on the dwellers of Chaldea.” This is a hurting people asking for the harm to land on the ones who did it. It's a heavy prayer.

Egypt isn't named in her words, friend. She says, “May the violence done to me and to my flesh be upon Babylon.” The one she's speaking about all through these verses is Babylon. Keep your eyes on the speaker's own words.

Edom isn't mentioned here, baker. The speaker says, “May the violence done to me and to my flesh be upon Babylon.” She also says, “May my blood be on the dwellers of Chaldea.” Both are aimed at Babylon and the people living there.

explanations.answer: Plead her case and take vengeance for her
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The LORD says, “Behold, I will plead your case and take vengeance on your behalf…” He answers Jerusalem's cry Himself. He doesn't hand it off to anyone else.

explanations.answer: Leave her case for the nations to settle
explanations.explanation: Close, since the nations are summoned in this passage. But the LORD says, “Behold, I will plead your case and take vengeance on your behalf.” He says "I," not the nations. He takes up her case Himself.

explanations.answer: Tell her to make peace with Babylon
explanations.explanation: He doesn't say anything like that here, friend. He answers her by saying, “Behold, I will plead your case and take vengeance on your behalf…” That's the LORD stepping in for her. There's no word about making peace in these verses.

You got it, baker. The LORD says, “Babylon will become a heap of rubble, a haunt for jackals…” Rubble is what's left of a city after it falls. The verse goes on to say it will be “an object of horror and scorn, without inhabitant.”

A heap of treasure would be a great find, friend, but that's not this verse. The LORD says, “Babylon will become a heap of rubble, a haunt for jackals.” Jackals are what move into an empty ruin. Nobody is digging for gold here.

Grain showed up earlier in the passage with the threshing floor, so I see the link. But this verse says, “Babylon will become a heap of rubble, a haunt for jackals.” A pile of rubble is what stays when a city is torn down. Jackals live in ruins, not in granaries.

explanations.answer: They fall asleep and never wake up
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The LORD says, “then they will fall asleep forever and never wake up, declares the LORD.” This is a sober line, and I won't joke about it. The feast comes first, and then the sleep that has no morning.

explanations.answer: They wake up and turn back to God
explanations.explanation: That's not what the verse says, friend. The LORD says they “will fall asleep forever and never wake up.” There is no waking in that line. It's a heavy word.

explanations.answer: They march out to fight the Medes
explanations.explanation: The Medes are in this passage, so I get why you'd think of them. But after the feast, the verse says, “then they will fall asleep forever and never wake up.” Nobody marches anywhere after that. It's a heavy ending, and the text says it plainly.

True, baker. The verse says, “The praise of all the earth has been seized. What a horror Babylon has become among the nations!” The city everyone once praised becomes something people look at with horror. That's quite a drop.

This one is true, friend. The verse says, “The praise of all the earth has been seized. What a horror Babylon has become among the nations!” So the text names both the praise and the horror. It's a big fall from one to the other.

This is false, baker. The verse says, “Her cities have become a desolation, a dry and arid land, a land where no one lives…” Dry and arid is the opposite of green fields. Those fields aren't in this picture.

That's right, friend. The verse says, “Her cities have become a desolation, a dry and arid land, a land where no one lives, where no son of man passes through.” Nothing green is growing there. It's empty and dry.

Yes, baker. The LORD says, “The nations will no longer stream to him…” Bel is a false god of Babylon, and the crowds that came to him will stop coming. The LORD is the one doing the punishing in this verse.

explanations.answer: They stream to him even more
explanations.explanation: It goes the other way, friend. The LORD says, “The nations will no longer stream to him…” That's a crowd that stops coming. More visitors would be the opposite of what the verse says.

explanations.answer: They stream to him from farther away
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say anything about distance, baker. It says, “The nations will no longer stream to him…” No longer means the crowd is gone, near or far. Bel doesn't get a bigger line out the door.
The wall doesn't stay up, friend. The LORD says, “even the wall of Babylon will fall.” The wall is one more thing that goes down. Nothing in this verse is left standing.
That's right, baker. The verse ends, “even the wall of Babylon will fall.” The word "even" tells you the wall was the kind of thing you'd expect to hold. But the LORD says it falls too.
